subject: Mixed
description: Medium-difficulty practice set (20 questions) covering: Anatomy, Biochemistry, Kinesio Therapeutics, Medicine, OBGY, Pathology & Microbiology, Pharmacology, Physiotherapy in Community Health, Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition, Physiotherapy in Neurosciences, Psychiatry, Psychology.

questions.question: The circle of Willis is clinically important in stroke because it:

options.A: Has no role in cerebral perfusion at all
options.B: Provides a collateral circulatory network that can help maintain blood flow if one contributing artery is occluded proximally
options.C: Is located exclusively in the spinal cord
options.D: Only supplies the cerebellum

questions.explanation: The circle of Willis connects the anterior and posterior cerebral circulations via communicating arteries, providing collateral blood flow. This is why occlusion proximal to the anterior or posterior communicating arteries often produces relatively minimal deficits — perfusion can be partly maintained from the other side.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Vascular Syndromes
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: Which hormone is chiefly responsible for the 'milk ejection' or 'let-down' reflex during breastfeeding?

options.B: Oxytocin
options.C: Progesterone
options.D: Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)

questions.explanation: Oxytocin is the major galactokinetic hormone: suckling triggers a neural reflex arc to the hypothalamus, causing oxytocin release from the posterior pituitary, which contracts the myoepithelial cells around the alveoli and ducts, forcing milk down into the lactiferous ducts (the 'let-down' reflex). Prolactin, by contrast, drives milk secretion itself (lactogenesis/galactopoiesis), not its ejection.
questions.sourceBook: Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Physiology of Lactation, Galactokinesis
questions.subject: OBGY

questions.question: Which type of necrosis is most commonly caused by sudden cessation of blood flow (ischaemia), classically affecting the heart, kidney, and spleen?

options.B: Coagulative necrosis
options.C: Caseous necrosis
options.D: Fat necrosis

questions.explanation: Coagulative necrosis is the most common type of necrosis, most often caused by sudden cessation of blood flow (ischaemic necrosis), typically affecting solid organs like the heart, kidney, and spleen — the classic example being a myocardial or renal infarct.
questions.sourceBook: Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology
questions.sourceChapter: Cell Injury, Cellular Adaptations and Cellular Ageing — Coagulative Necrosis
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: Social phobia is characterised primarily by fear of:

options.B: One's own actions being critically viewed by others, leading to embarrassment or humiliation
options.C: A single specific, well-circumscribed object like spiders or heights
options.D: Contamination by dirt or germs

questions.explanation: Social phobia is an irrational fear of performing activities in front of others or interacting socially, driven by fear that one's own actions will be judged critically, leading to embarrassment (examples include fear of public speaking, blushing, or eating in front of others).
questions.sourceBook: Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry
questions.sourceChapter: Neurotic, Stress-related and Somatoform Disorders — Phobic Disorder
questions.subject: Psychiatry

questions.question: The hypothalamus regulates the body's internal environment (temperature, blood salt concentration, hormone levels) chiefly by controlling secretions from which gland?

options.B: The pituitary gland
options.C: The adrenal gland directly, bypassing the pituitary entirely
options.D: The pancreas

questions.explanation: The hypothalamus is connected to the pituitary gland and controls its hormone secretion into the bloodstream, either through nerve impulses or chemical releasing factors — linking the nervous system to the body's broader glandular (endocrine) system.
questions.sourceBook: Morgan & King, Introduction to Psychology
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Forebrain: Hypothalamus and Pituitary
questions.subject: Psychology

questions.question: Damage to the motor cortex on the LEFT side of the brain will typically produce movement weakness on which side of the body?

options.B: The right side (opposite side), because motor fibers cross to the other side below the head
options.C: Both sides equally
options.D: Neither side — motor cortex damage never affects limb movement

questions.explanation: Fibers from the motor cortex on one side of the brain cross to the opposite side of the body on their way down to the spinal cord. So damage to the left motor cortex produces weakness, loss of dexterity, or spastic paralysis on the right side of the body below the head.
questions.sourceBook: Morgan & King, Introduction to Psychology
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Sensory and Motor Functions
questions.subject: Psychology

questions.question: Corticosteroid use weakening host defence mechanisms and allowing reactivation of latent tuberculosis is an example of which category of adverse drug effect?

options.B: A secondary effect (an indirect consequence of the drug's primary action)
options.C: Drug idiosyncrasy
options.D: A Type I hypersensitivity reaction

questions.explanation: Secondary effects are indirect consequences of a drug's primary action — corticosteroids' primary immunosuppressive action indirectly allows latent infections like tuberculosis to reactivate, and similarly, tetracyclines suppressing normal bacterial flora can indirectly permit superinfections.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Adverse Drug Effects — Classification
questions.subject: Pharmacology

questions.question: Training to improve muscular (local) endurance typically involves:

options.A: A very heavy load for only 1-2 repetitions
options.B: Many repetitions (e.g. 3-5 sets of 40-50 reps) against a low, submaximal load
options.C: A single maximal isometric contraction held for 1 second
options.D: Complete rest with no muscular activity

questions.explanation: Muscle endurance training involves performing many repetitions against a submaximal load — for example, as many as three to five sets of 40 to 50 repetitions against a low resistance — and can be safely initiated early in rehabilitation since the load involved is low.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — To Improve Muscle Endurance
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: Which of the following is a correct characteristic of the peptide bond?

options.A: It is highly flexible and freely rotates
options.B: It is rigid and planar, with partial double-bond character, generally existing in the trans configuration
options.C: It cannot participate in hydrogen bonding
options.D: It only forms between two acidic amino acids

questions.explanation: The peptide bond (C=O to N-H) has partial double-bond character, which makes it rigid and planar rather than freely rotating, and it generally exists in the trans configuration. Both the C=O and N-H groups are polar and participate in hydrogen bond formation, which is important for secondary structure.
questions.sourceBook: Satyanarayana, Biochemistry
questions.sourceChapter: Proteins and Amino Acids — Peptide Bond
questions.subject: Biochemistry

questions.question: In epidemiological studies, 'comparability' between study and control groups is best ensured by:

options.A: Choosing groups of very different ages and backgrounds to maximise contrast
options.B: Randomization or random allocation, or 'matching' for selected characteristics when random allocation is not possible (e.g. case-control/cohort studies)
options.C: Always excluding any consideration of age or sex
options.D: Comparability is not actually necessary for valid epidemiological conclusions

questions.explanation: Comparability ('like being compared with like') between study and control groups is best ensured by randomization or random allocation. Where this is not possible, such as in case-control or cohort studies, 'matching' for selected characteristics is used instead, and standardization can address a limited number of characteristics like age, sex, and parity.
questions.sourceBook: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Epidemiology and Epidemiologic Methods — Making Comparisons
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Community Health

questions.question: According to the objectives of postpartum exercise, which muscle groups are specifically targeted to prevent genital prolapse and stress incontinence of urine?

options.B: The abdominal and pelvic floor muscles
options.C: The cervical extensors only
options.D: The quadriceps exclusively

questions.explanation: Postpartum exercises aim to improve tone of the abdominal and perineal (pelvic floor) muscles, which are stretched during pregnancy and labour. Effective pelvic floor exercise specifically helps prevent genital prolapse and stress urinary incontinence.
questions.sourceBook: Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Postpartum Exercise
questions.subject: OBGY

questions.question: 'Overconfidence bias' in clinical decision-making refers to:

options.A: The tendency to always order more diagnostic tests than necessary
options.B: The tendency to believe one knows more than one actually does, placing too much faith in opinion over gathered evidence
options.C: A bias that only affects junior doctors, never senior clinicians
options.D: Excessive reliance on clinical prediction rules

questions.explanation: Overconfidence bias is the tendency to place too much faith in one's own opinion rather than the gathered evidence, sometimes compounded further by availability bias and commission bias (a tendency to act rather than not act), occasionally with serious consequences.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Clinical Decision Making — Common Cognitive Biases
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: The ulna is often described as the 'stabilising bone' of the forearm because:

options.A: Its trochlear notch grips the lower end of the humerus, giving the radius a stable foundation from which to pronate and supinate
options.B: It is the only bone that moves during pronation/supination
options.C: It bears the entire weight of the upper limb at the wrist joint
options.D: It has no muscular attachments, unlike the radius

questions.explanation: The ulna's trochlear notch grips the lower end of the humerus at the elbow, forming a stable hinge. This gives the radius the fixed foundation it needs to rotate around the ulna for efficient pronation and supination of the hand.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Clinical Anatomy
questions.subject: Anatomy

questions.question: Following moderate-intensity resistance training, what rest period is generally recommended between sets?

options.B: 2 to 3 minutes
options.C: 24 hours
options.D: No rest is needed between sets

questions.explanation: For moderate-intensity resistance training, a 2- to 3-minute rest period between sets is generally recommended, with longer rest periods (>3 minutes) needed for high-intensity training of large, multi-joint muscle groups.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Rest Interval
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: The lateral intermuscular septum of the thigh, the thickest of the three septa, separates which two compartments?

options.A: The anterior compartment from the posterior compartment
options.B: The medial compartment from the posterior compartment
options.C: The anterior compartment from the medial compartment
options.D: It does not separate any compartments

questions.explanation: The lateral intermuscular septum, the thickest of the thigh's three intermuscular septa, extends from the iliotibial tract to the lateral lip of the linea aspera and separates the anterior compartment of the thigh from the posterior compartment.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Lower Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Front of Thigh — Intermuscular Septa
questions.subject: Anatomy

questions.question: The 'unpacking principle' in clinical reasoning refers to the risk that:

options.A: A failure to fully take the history and examine the patient means important information can be missed, leading to error
options.B: Patients should always be admitted for observation regardless of findings
options.C: Clinical prediction rules should never be used
options.D: Diagnostic tests are always more reliable than clinical examination

questions.explanation: The unpacking principle highlights that history-taking and physical examination, though seemingly obvious steps, are sometimes performed inadequately — and this failure to 'unpack' all the available information can cause important findings to be missed.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Clinical Decision Making — Reducing Errors, Cognitive Debiasing Strategies
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: Hughston's posteromedial drawer sign is performed with the patient supine, knee flexed 80-90°, hip flexed 45°, and the foot slightly medially rotated. A positive test (excessive posterior movement/rotation of the medial tibia) is most indicative of injury to which primary structure?

options.B: Posterior cruciate ligament (along with posteromedial supporting structures)
options.C: Lateral collateral ligament only
options.D: Iliotibial band

questions.explanation: A positive Hughston's posteromedial drawer sign indicates injury to the posterior cruciate ligament, along with possible involvement of the posterior oblique ligament, medial collateral ligament, semimembranosus, and posteromedial capsule — it tests for posteromedial rotary instability of the knee.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — Ligament Stability, Posteromedial and Posterolateral Drawer Sign
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: When multiple muscle groups are exercised in a single session, the recommended order is generally:

options.A: Small muscle groups before large muscle groups, single-joint before multi-joint exercises
options.B: Large muscle groups before small muscle groups, and multi-joint exercises before single-joint exercises
options.C: Order makes no difference to fatigue or training effect
options.D: Lower intensity exercises should always precede higher intensity ones, regardless of warm-up

questions.explanation: The recommended exercise order is large muscle groups before small muscle groups, and multi-joint exercises before single-joint exercises, with higher-intensity exercises performed before lower-intensity ones after an appropriate warm-up.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Exercise Order
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: Insulin and epidermal growth factor (EGF) act through which type of receptor?

options.B: Ligand-gated ion channels
options.C: Receptor tyrosine kinases (transmembrane enzyme-linked receptors)
options.D: Cytoplasmic nuclear receptors

questions.explanation: Insulin, EGF, and many other growth factors act through receptor tyrosine kinases: hormone binding causes receptor dimerization, activating an intracellular tyrosine kinase domain that autophosphorylates and triggers downstream signalling — a process that plays out over minutes to hours, much slower than ion-channel receptors.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Mechanism of Drug Action; Receptor Pharmacology
questions.subject: Pharmacology

questions.question: A key diagnostic criterion for anorexia nervosa is a Quetelet's body-mass index (BMI) of:

options.B: 25 or more
options.C: 30 or more
options.D: BMI is irrelevant to the diagnosis

questions.explanation: One diagnostic criterion for anorexia nervosa is significant weight loss (usually more than 25% of original weight), with the final weight typically 15% below the minimum normal weight for age/sex/height, or a BMI of 17.5 or less.
questions.sourceBook: Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry
questions.sourceChapter: Eating Disorders — Anorexia Nervosa
questions.subject: Psychiatry
